nameStory: The Polyphemus moth gets its dramatic name from Greek mythology, specifically the one-eyed giant cyclops Polyphemus who was famously outwitted by Odysseus. The moth's spectacular eyespots on its hindwings reminded early naturalists of that legendary single eye. When threatened, the moth can flash these large, staring 'eyes' to startle predators, just like the fearsome gaze of its mythical namesake.
description: The Polyphemus moth is one of New England's most impressive native moths, belonging to the giant silk moth family. With wings spanning up to 6 inches across, it's truly a giant among our local moths. The moth displays warm tan and brown colors overall, but its most striking feature is the pair of large, purplish eyespots adorning its hindwings. These beautiful moths are active at night and are often attracted to porch lights during their flight season.

idTips.label: Large purple eyespots
idTips.description: Each hindwing features a prominent eyespot with a dark purple center ringed in yellow and black - these are impossible to miss and unlike any other New England moth

idTips.label: Impressive size
idTips.description: Wingspan reaches 6 inches, making it one of our largest moths - bigger than many small birds and easily noticed when resting on tree trunks or walls

idTips.label: Tan and brown coloration
idTips.description: Overall warm brown and tan tones with subtle darker banding across the wings, giving it excellent camouflage against tree bark

idTips.label: Fuzzy, robust body
idTips.description: The body is thick and densely covered in soft, tan-colored fur-like scales that feel almost woolly to the touch

idTips.label: Feathery antennae
idTips.description: Males have particularly elaborate, feather-like antennae that look almost fern-like and are used to detect female pheromones from miles away

habitat: Look for Polyphemus moths in deciduous hardwood forests, orchards, suburban areas with mature trees, and wetland edges throughout New England. They thrive wherever their caterpillars can find host trees like oak, maple, birch, cherry, and willow. You're most likely to spot adults near porch lights, streetlights, or resting on tree trunks during the day in both rural and urban settings.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge in late spring, typically May into early June. Look for large brown cocoons wrapped in leaves that have overwintered on trees and shrubs.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight season occurs in early to mid-summer when adults are active at night, mating and laying eggs. This is your best chance to see them at lights or find them resting during the day.
seasonality.fall: Large, bright green caterpillars with orange tubercles are feeding heavily on deciduous trees, growing dramatically before pupating. Look for them munching on oak, maple, and other hardwood leaves.
seasonality.winter: Moths overwinter as pupae inside tough, brown cocoons attached to branches. The cocoons are easier to spot on bare winter trees and feel papery to the touch.

funFact: Polyphemus caterpillars are eating machines that consume 86,000 times their original body weight in just 56 days - that's like a 7-pound human baby eating over 300 tons of food in two months!
confusionNotes: The large eyespots make this moth nearly unmistakable, but it might be confused with the smaller Io moth, which has similar eyespots. Remember: Polyphemus has eyespots only on the hindwings and is much larger overall, while Io moths have eyespots on both front and back wings and are considerably smaller.
contextualKnowledge: Despite their impressive size and dramatic appearance, adult Polyphemus moths don't have functioning mouths and cannot eat - they live off stored energy from their caterpillar stage and focus entirely on finding mates and reproducing during their brief adult life of just a week or two.
compareHints: Polyphemus is the only member of its genus (Antheraea) found in New England, making it unique among our local giant silk moths. Compared to other large moths in the Saturniidae family like the Cecropia moth, Polyphemus is smaller and has the distinctive purple eyespots rather than the red, white, and crescent-shaped markings of its relatives. The eyespot pattern is truly one-of-a-kind in our region.
